title: The bond continues
hookLine: many keep a bond with the dead, and grief researchers now see it as healthy

lines: A TEXT TO A NUMBER THAT WON'T ANSWER.
cards: A phone, a name in the contacts, and a message sent anyway: got the job. wish you could see. Nobody will answer. She knows that.

She sends it anyway, puts the phone down, and feels a little less alone with the news. Somewhere else a man sets out his father's chair at the holiday table. A woman tells a gravestone about the new baby.
For a long time, some schools of psychology would have called all of this a problem, a sign of grief not finished. What changed, and what were some traditions doing all along?

teach.h: LET GO, SAID AN OLDER VIEW
teach.b: First, the older view. Healthy grief meant letting go: slowly loosening your ties to the person who died, so your heart was free to attach elsewhere. Some trace the idea to Freud's essay Mourning and Melancholia.
Keeping up a relationship with the dead could look like refusing to accept the death. Second, the turn.
The researchers Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman and Steven Nickman gathered studies of grieving people in a book called Continuing Bonds.

People kept a relationship with their dead: talking to them, asking what they would think, carrying their values, feeling them near at a wedding. And this was often part of healthy grieving, not a failure of it.
Researchers since have added a fair caution: some bonds comfort and some trouble, depending on the person and the loss. Third, traditions had words for this already.

teach.h: MAY THEIR MEMORY BE A BLESSING
teach.b: In Jewish custom, after naming someone who has died, people add a short phrase: may their memory be a blessing.
In some Japanese Buddhist homes, a household altar called a butsudan holds photos and memorial tablets, and families greet the dead there, offer rice or tea, and tell them the news.
Fourth, what continues is not the same as what was.
The bond changes shape: from a voice on the phone to a voice in memory, from advice given to advice imagined, from a hand held to a value carried. The relationship moves. It doesn't have to end.

how: People keep bonds with the dead in many ways: Jewish families add "may their memory be a blessing" after a name, some Japanese Buddhist households greet the dead at a home altar, and others visit graves, keep a photo, or talk to the person on a walk.

o: a home altar where a family greets its dead
a temple bell rung once for each death
a family grave where the ashes are kept

games.q: what keeps the bond — tap the pairs.
p: let go so the heart is free
talking to the dead can be healthy
may his memory be a blessing
a home altar where the dead hear news

s: the Continuing Bonds researchers found a bond with the dead can be healthy
they found people kept relationships with their dead, often as part of healthy grieving.
a continuing bond means refusing to accept the death
the bond changes shape: from presence to memory, conversation and values.
researchers say every bond with the dead brings comfort
they add a caution: some bonds comfort and some trouble.

games.q: a friend tells you she still talks to her late father on her morning walks. what do you do?
o: tell her it's time to let go.
ask her what she tells him.
games.why: grief researchers now see bonds like this as often healthy; asking about it honors the relationship that's still going.

practice: Choose someone who has died, a person or even an animal, or if no one comes, an ancestor you never met, and let them come to mind as they were on an ordinary day.
Silently tell them one thing, a piece of news, a thank-you, a question, then simply sit, the way you would after saying something to a friend across the table, no answer needed.
If you pray, you can pray for them in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Butsudan, the household altar in some Japanese Buddhist homes where family members greet their dead and tell them the news. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew, said after naming a man who has died: may his memory be a blessing (for a woman, zikhronah).

carryVoice: Your line: a voice in memory. Staying in touch can take a new shape. Eight hundred days now.
